questions.q: In the code below, an exception is thrown just before the second flush(). What is left in the database?
questions.hint: How many transactions does each flush() run, and when is each one committed?

options.text: The order stays paid, but no money is taken from the wallet
options.why: The first flush() was committed earlier as its own transaction. A later exception can no longer undo it.

options.text: Both changes roll back on their own
options.why: Rollback only undoes the changes of a running transaction. The first flush()'s transaction ended long ago.

options.text: Nothing is saved, because Doctrine saves everything together at the end of the request
options.why: Doctrine doesn't wait for the end of the request; the SQL is sent and committed the moment flush() is called.

options.text: Money is taken from the wallet, but the order stays pending
options.why: The other way around. withdraw() only changed the entity in memory; the second flush() never ran, so it never reached the database.

questions.q: When a transaction is rolled back, which of these return to their earlier state?
questions.hint: Which things does the database keep track of, and which are out of its reach?

options.text: An UPDATE made in that transaction
options.why: The database erases every change of the same transaction itself. That is Atomicity.

options.text: An INSERT made in that transaction
options.why: A new row is part of the transaction too; after a rollback it was never there.

options.text: An email sent from inside the transaction
options.why: The mail server isn't part of the database transaction. Once sent, an email can't be recalled.

options.text: A charge made at a payment gateway from inside the transaction
options.why: The gateway is a separate system. Your database rollback tells it nothing; you would have to issue a refund separately.

options.text: A value written to the Redis cache from inside the transaction
options.why: Redis is a separate system; a rollback in the SQL database doesn't reach it, and the stale value stays.

questions.q: The balance column has CHECK (balance >= 0). A transaction tries to set a balance to −100 and the database refuses to commit. Which ACID promise is this?
questions.hint: Here a declared rule is being enforced.

options.text: Atomicity
options.why: Atomicity says all steps happen or none do. The point here is refusing to let a rule be broken.

options.text: Consistency
options.why: The database refuses to store a state that violates a declared constraint. That is Consistency.

options.text: Isolation
options.why: Isolation is about how concurrent transactions affect each other; here there is only one transaction.

options.text: Durability
options.why: Durability says committed data survives a crash. Here nothing is being committed at all.

questions.q: Sarah's handler changes three entities and calls flush() once at the end. The third UPDATE violates a constraint. What happens to the first two?
questions.hint: How does flush() send the pending changes?

options.text: The first two stay saved, only the third is dropped
options.why: That would leave a half-done state. flush() runs all the changes in one transaction precisely to prevent it.

options.text: They roll back too, because flush() runs all changes in one transaction
options.why: flush() does its own BEGIN … COMMIT. If one SQL statement fails, everything rolls back and the EntityManager is closed.

options.text: Doctrine fixes the third one and retries automatically
options.why: Doctrine neither fixes nor retries anything; it throws the exception.

questions.q: Which statements about wrapInTransaction() are true?
questions.hint: What does it do inside the database, and what is beyond its reach?

options.text: It calls flush() and COMMIT itself when the closure ends
options.why: So you don't write a separate flush() inside, and you also get the closure's return value back.

options.text: On an exception it issues ROLLBACK and closes the EntityManager
options.why: After a failed transaction the state of the in-memory entities can no longer be trusted, so the EntityManager is closed.

options.text: It also rolls back an HTTP call made from inside
options.why: It only undoes database changes; whatever went out to an outside system is beyond its reach.

options.text: It automatically queues up two requests that touch the same row
options.why: Queueing requests takes a lock (for example PESSIMISTIC_WRITE). With only a transaction, both can read the same stale value at once.

questions.q: A transaction calls an SMS gateway that sometimes takes 20 seconds. What is the biggest risk?
questions.hint: During those 20 seconds, what state is the database transaction in?

options.text: The database will commit the transaction by itself after 20 seconds
options.why: The database never commits on its own; the transaction stays open until your code says otherwise.

options.text: The transaction stays open holding locks, so other requests pile up on those rows
options.why: A long transaction means long locks. Under load the waiting requests accumulate until the whole site slows down.

options.text: There is no risk; the longer the transaction, the safer the data
options.why: The opposite: the shorter the transaction, the less time locks are held. Safety comes from the right boundaries, not from length.

options.text: If the SMS fails, the database will retry sending it
options.why: The database knows nothing about SMS. Retrying needs a queue and a worker.

questions.q: Two requests simultaneously read the same wallet balance, calculate and write. Both are inside wrapInTransaction(), but there is no lock. What can happen?
questions.hint: Which balance did each of them see at the start?

options.text: Because there is a transaction, the second waits for the first by itself
options.why: A plain SELECT takes no lock, so both read the same value at once.

options.text: The database cancels both transactions
options.why: At the default isolation level the database sees no problem here and lets both commit.

options.text: One overwrites the other's change, so the balance ends up wrong
options.why: Both calculated from the same stale balance, and whoever writes last wins. This is a lost update.

options.text: The data is lost after the commit
options.why: Durability works fine: the wrong value is stored permanently.

questions.q: In a report transaction, the first query returns a total due of $500, and the next query's list sums to $400. The database is PostgreSQL with default settings. What is the simplest fix?
questions.hint: The two queries must see the picture of one moment. Which level provides that?

options.text: Call flush() between the two queries
options.why: flush() sends Doctrine's pending changes; it has no effect on how your queries see other transactions' commits.

options.text: Run the report transaction at REPEATABLE READ
options.why: Then the whole transaction sees one snapshot from the start, so the total and the list always agree.

options.text: Run the two queries outside the transaction
options.why: Each query would then be its own transaction: the same problem, no improvement.

options.text: Block all writes to the customer table while the report runs
options.why: It would work, but every payment in the shop would be stuck for as long as the report runs. A snapshot gives the same result without blocking anyone.

questions.q: Transaction A marks an order "paid" but hasn't committed. Transaction B sees "paid" and ships the goods. Then A rolls back. Which anomaly did B fall victim to?
questions.hint: Was the value B read ever confirmed?

options.text: Dirty read
options.why: B read another transaction's uncommitted change, which was later rolled back.

options.text: Non-repeatable read
options.why: That is reading the same row twice and getting two different committed values. Here the value B read was never committed at all.

options.text: Phantom read
options.why: A phantom means new rows appearing under the same condition; no new rows are involved here.

options.text: Lost update
options.why: In a lost update, one write wipes out another. Here the problem is reading something wrong, not losing a write.

questions.q: A clinic's rule: at least one doctor must be on call. Two doctors simultaneously see 2 on call, then each writes on_call = false on their own row. Now nobody is on call. Which anomaly is this?
questions.hint: Did the two write the same row, or different rows?

options.text: Lost update
options.why: No write was lost; both writes are stored, because they changed different rows.

options.text: Dirty read
options.why: Both read correct committed data (2 people). The problem isn't in the reading, but in both writing at once on the strength of it.

options.text: Write skew
options.why: Two decisions based on the same facts were written to different rows; each is valid alone, but together they break the rule.

options.text: Non-repeatable read
options.why: Nobody read the same row twice. This is a write problem, not a read problem.

questions.q: Which of these can happen at PostgreSQL's default level (READ COMMITTED)?
questions.hint: This level guarantees just one thing: you won't see unconfirmed writes.

options.text: Dirty read
options.why: The name says it: READ COMMITTED lets you read only committed data.

options.text: Non-repeatable read
options.why: Every query looks afresh, so reading the same row again can return a changed value.

options.text: Lost update
options.why: If two transactions read the same stale value and write back, the later one wipes out the earlier; this level does not stop that.

options.text: Write skew
options.why: Only SERIALIZABLE prevents write skew; it can happen at every level below it.

options.text: Phantom read
options.why: If someone adds a row and commits between your two queries, the second query sees it.

questions.q: This code correctly sets SERIALIZABLE. Yet under load, users occasionally get a 500 error. What is missing?
questions.hint: What does SERIALIZABLE do when it detects a collision?

options.text: Writing COMMIT by hand after the UPDATE
options.why: transactional() commits by itself when the closure ends; that isn't missing.

options.text: Catching the serialization failure and rerunning the whole transaction
options.why: On a collision the database aborts a transaction. If you don't catch the RetryableException and rerun, that abort reaches the user as a 500.

options.text: Lowering the level to READ UNCOMMITTED so collisions can't happen
options.why: The errors would go away, but write skew would return: both people would take leave.

options.text: Moving the SELECT outside the transaction
options.why: Then the database could not see how the read relates to the write, and could no longer catch write skew.

questions.q: A transaction at REPEATABLE READ reads due = 500 from a row at the start. Another transaction then changes it to 300 and commits. What does the first transaction see when it reads the same row again?
questions.hint: If you write on the original ledger after taking a photocopy, does the photocopy change?

options.text: 300, because that was committed
options.why: That is READ COMMITTED behavior, where every query looks afresh.

options.text: 500, because it sees the snapshot from the start of the transaction
options.why: At REPEATABLE READ the whole transaction sees one frozen picture; whatever others commit later is not visible.

options.text: An error, because the row has changed
options.why: Merely reading raises no error. PostgreSQL raises one when this transaction tries to write that changed row.

options.text: NULL, because the row is locked
options.why: The other transaction has already committed, so there is no lock; and even with a lock the result wouldn't be NULL.

questions.q: Which statements about the SERIALIZABLE level are true?
questions.hint: Think about both the benefit and the price of the strictest level.

options.text: It prevents every anomaly, including write skew
options.why: The result is as if the transactions ran one after another, so there is no room for any anomaly.

options.text: A transaction may be aborted, so you need retry
options.why: When the database detects a collision it fails one transaction with a serialization failure; handling that is the application's job.

options.text: It is the default in both PostgreSQL and MySQL
options.why: PostgreSQL defaults to READ COMMITTED and MySQL InnoDB to REPEATABLE READ.

options.text: Making it the default for the whole app costs nothing
options.why: More aborts and retries slow things down. Use it only for the transactions whose rule spans several rows.

questions.q: What can go wrong if two requests run this code at the same time?
questions.hint: What value do both requests start their calculation from?

options.text: Both read the same stock and write the same new value, so one sale is lost from the count
options.why: This is read-modify-write. Both read 10 and write 9, when the correct value is 8.

options.text: Doctrine automatically makes the second request wait
options.why: Doctrine does nothing of the kind; without a lock, both run at the same time.

options.text: The second flush() always throws an exception
options.why: No constraint is violated, so flush() succeeds; it is only the arithmetic that comes out wrong.

options.text: Nothing, because flush() uses a transaction
options.why: A transaction prevents half-done work, but it doesn't stop two transactions from reading the same stale value.

questions.q: Which change closes the gap in the wallet code from the first slide?
questions.hint: Which version leaves no moment between the check and the write?

options.text: One UPDATE … SET balance = balance - ? WHERE id = ? AND balance >= ?, treating 0 changed rows as "insufficient funds"
options.why: The check and the subtraction happen in one statement, so phone 2 sees 200, matches no row and is refused.

options.text: Read the balance a second time just before writing
options.why: A second read is just another gap. Someone can still write between it and your write.

options.text: Keep the PHP check and add usleep() before the write
options.why: Waiting only shifts the timing; both requests can still read the same stale balance.

options.text: Add a unique constraint on wallet.id
options.why: The id is already unique, and no duplicate row is involved. The trouble is two writes to the same row.

questions.q: Which of these are examples of a check-then-act race condition?
questions.hint: Ask of each one: is there a "look first, then act" in it?

options.text: Booking a seat after seeing it is free
options.why: Between the look and the booking, someone else can take the seat.

options.text: Deducting money after seeing the balance is enough
options.why: If the balance you saw has gone stale, money that doesn't exist gets spent.

options.text: Creating a new account after seeing the email is unused
options.why: In the gap between the check and the creation, someone can register with the same email.

options.text: Validating every field of a form before sending a response
options.why: No shared database state is read and then written, so there is no gap against other requests.

questions.q: Ryan may use a coupon only once. He taps from two tabs at the same time and gets it twice. The code is `if (!$used) { apply(); $used = true; }`. What is the real problem?
questions.hint: What happened between the check and the change?

options.text: Both requests saw `$used` as false
options.why: The second one read before the first had written true. That is the check-then-act gap.

options.text: The server's clock is wrong
options.why: The clock has nothing to do with it; the error comes from the steps of two requests interleaving.

options.text: The coupon table has no index
options.why: An index makes queries faster, not correct. Even with an index, both would read the same value.

options.text: The user's browser is out of date
options.why: The problem is in the server's database, not the browser. A direct API call would behave the same.

questions.q: You fire twenty $100 requests at once at a $1,000 wallet, and 13 succeed. What could the final balance be?
questions.hint: What did each successful request write, and does the last write win?

options.text: Exactly 0
options.why: The correct arithmetic would give 0, but more than 10 successes means some requests wrote from the same stale value, so the balance usually isn't 0.

options.text: Most likely above zero, even though $1,300 went out
options.why: Some requests wiped out each other's writes (lost updates), so the balance shows more than it should: $300 was created from nothing.

options.text: Definitely −300
options.why: It can't go below 0: every request checked for at least 100 before writing, so no write is negative. Lost updates push the balance up, not down.

questions.q: To keep emails unique, a colleague says "just check with findOneBy before registering". Which view is right?
questions.hint: Where would a guard have to sit for all requests to meet at one place?

options.text: That works, because PHP handles one request at a time
options.why: Several worker processes run at once; a single thread inside PHP doesn't prevent that.

options.text: It will work if you add usleep() after findOneBy
options.why: Waiting doesn't shrink the gap, it only shifts the timing. The race remains.

options.text: It isn't enough; you need a unique constraint on email and you must catch the exception
options.why: The database lines up every insert and lets only one survive. findOneBy is only good for giving a nicer error message.

options.text: Keeping the used emails in a static variable will do
options.why: A static variable is separate for each process; other workers and servers don't see it.

questions.q: Which approaches do NOT reliably prevent a race condition?
questions.hint: A method confined to one process or one browser can't see every request.

options.text: Disabling the submit button
options.why: It is only UX. A direct API call, a retry or a second device walks right around it.

options.text: Keeping a PHP static flag
options.why: The flag lives in each process's own memory; other workers and servers know nothing about it.

options.text: Adding a unique constraint
options.why: This is a reliable approach: the database itself blocks duplicate inserts.

options.text: Running a conditional atomic UPDATE
options.why: When the read and the write happen in one SQL statement, there is no gap in between, so this is reliable too.

questions.q: What goes wrong when two requests run this code at the same time, and what does it need to be fixed?
questions.hint: Is there any lock on the row while it is being read?

options.text: There is no lock, so both read the same balance; the find must use PESSIMISTIC_WRITE inside a transaction
options.why: The balance read after the lock is the true one, because other requests wait in line until the commit.

options.text: Nothing is wrong, because flush() uses a transaction
options.why: flush()'s transaction wraps only the write, not the balance that was read earlier.

options.text: Checking the balance with another if will be enough
options.why: A second look is just another gap; with no lock, someone can still slip in between the check and the write.

options.text: Wrapping it in try/catch will be enough
options.why: Catching exceptions doesn't stop the race, because no exception is being thrown here at all.

questions.q: Where is an optimistic lock the best fit?
questions.hint: How long does the user keep the form open, and how often do collisions happen?

options.text: A wallet balance with many transactions per second
options.why: With frequent collisions, optimistic locking piles up failures and retries; pessimistic locking or an atomic update is better here.

options.text: Editing a product in an admin panel, where the form stays open for minutes
options.why: You can't hold a lock while the form is open; comparing versions catches the conflict at save time.

options.text: Many people buying the last ticket for a seat at once
options.why: Everyone is fighting over the same row, so there would be many failures. A lock or an atomic update is needed here.

options.text: A cron job that must run only once
options.why: There is no row here at all; you need a lock by name (Symfony Lock or an advisory lock).

questions.q: What happens when this code runs?
questions.hint: Where does a pessimistic lock work, and where doesn't it?

options.text: A TransactionRequiredException, because there is no open transaction
options.why: A pessimistic lock requires a transaction. Wrap the code in wrapInTransaction().

options.text: The row is locked and released on its own after flush()
options.why: Without a transaction, the exception comes straight from find(); it never gets as far as taking the lock.

options.text: The lock does nothing and execution quietly continues
options.why: Doctrine throws an explicit exception here, so you can't run without the lock by accident.

questions.q: Sarah and Rob both open the same product at version 3. Sarah saves. What happens when Rob saves?
questions.hint: What is the row's version after Sarah's save?

options.text: Rob's change overwrites Sarah's
options.why: That would happen without an optimistic lock. Comparing versions prevents it.

options.text: Sarah's change merges with Rob's automatically
options.why: Doctrine doesn't merge anything. It only reports the conflict.

options.text: Rob's save gets an OptimisticLockException, because the version is now 4
options.why: WHERE version = 3 now finds no row, and Rob is told to reload.

questions.q: A shop has 50 tickets and 200 buyers click Buy in the first second. Which approaches fit?
questions.hint: Do most requests collide, and how long is the work between read and write?

options.text: A pessimistic lock on the ticket stock row
options.why: Nearly every request collides and the work is short, so queueing for the row is cheap and gives correct counts.

options.text: An optimistic lock with a version column
options.why: Almost all of the 200 would collide, fail and retry, then collide again. That is a pile of wasted work.

options.text: One UPDATE … SET stock = stock - 1 WHERE stock > 0
options.why: It is atomic on its own: the database checks and subtracts in one step, so no lock code is needed.

options.text: No lock: read the stock, check it, then save
options.why: That is the check-then-act gap. Several buyers read "1 left" together and all get a ticket.

questions.q: Which of these are reasonable places to use Symfony Lock or an advisory lock?
questions.hint: Where is there no separate row to lock?

options.text: A cron job running on several servers that must run only once
options.why: If every server asks for the same named lock, only one gets it, and the rest skip the job.

options.text: Making sure the monthly invoice export doesn't run twice at once
options.why: The job has no specific row of its own, so a lock by name fits.

options.text: Making sure two requests don't deduct the same wallet balance twice
options.why: Here there is a row; a row lock or an atomic UPDATE is simpler and safer, and has no TTL risk.

options.text: Keeping emails unique
options.why: A database unique constraint is the most reliable tool for that.

questions.q: When two transfers run in opposite directions at the same time, you sometimes get a "Deadlock found" error. What is the first remedy?
questions.hint: Who is waiting for whom, and in what order?

options.text: Follow one lock order everywhere, smaller id first
options.why: With one order, an opposite-direction cycle can't form; this is the root cause of deadlocks.

options.text: Stop taking locks at all
options.why: Removing the locks would remove the deadlock but bring the race back, and balances would be wrong again.

options.text: Add more work inside the transaction
options.why: More work inside means locks are held longer, which gives deadlocks more chances.

options.text: Reduce the number of database connections
options.why: That adds waiting, but it does nothing about the cause of the cycle.

questions.q: Stock is 1. Two requests run the code below at the same time. What can the final state be?
questions.hint: What stock value did each of them read?

options.text: Both read stock 1, and two orders can be confirmed: one phone, two sales
options.why: There is a gap between the read and the write. Both read 1 and wrote 0, and neither failed.

options.text: The second flush() throws an exception because stock goes negative
options.why: Both write 0, not −1. No constraint is violated.

options.text: Doctrine cancels one of them itself
options.why: Doctrine takes no lock and cancels nothing; fixing that is up to you.

questions.q: Which of these are correct ways to decrement stock?
questions.hint: Look for the ones where the condition and the decrement are in one step.

options.text: Run `UPDATE product SET stock = stock - 1 WHERE id = 7 AND stock >= 1` and check affected rows
options.why: The condition and the change are in one step, and you decide from the result. There is no gap for a race.

options.text: Load with PESSIMISTIC_WRITE inside wrapInTransaction(), check stock, then decrement
options.why: The row lock closes the gap. Others wait in line, though it is heavier than an atomic UPDATE.

options.text: Read stock, check it with an `if`, then `setStock($s - 1)`
options.why: That is read-modify-write; there is no lock, so the gap remains.

options.text: Count stock with a PHP static counter
options.why: A static variable is separate in every process; other workers don't see it.

questions.q: Two webhooks simultaneously run `UPDATE orders SET status='paid' WHERE id=12 AND status='pending'`. What are the second one's affected rows, and what should it do?
questions.hint: After the first one changed the status, does the WHERE still match?

options.text: 1, and it sends the receipt too
options.why: The status is already paid by then, so the WHERE doesn't match. If it were 1, the receipt would go out twice.

options.text: 0; it realizes the work is done and quietly returns success
options.why: This is the safe behavior for a duplicate webhook: the work happens once, and the response is 200 both times.

options.text: An exception, because two UPDATEs may not run at the same time
options.why: The database runs the two serially, with no exception; the second one just changes nothing.

questions.q: What is the most reliable way to guarantee one vote per poll?
questions.hint: Where do all the requests meet?

options.text: Check with `findOneBy(poll, user)` before voting
options.why: Another vote can slip in between the check and the insert; that is a race.

options.text: Disable the button in the frontend
options.why: That is only UX; a direct API call walks around it.

options.text: Add `UNIQUE (poll_id, user_id)` and catch the exception
options.why: The database lines up every insert and lets only one survive.

options.text: Keep the voters in a PHP static array
options.why: Process memory isn't shared with other workers and is gone after a restart.

questions.q: Which of these are good places to use an upsert?
questions.hint: Where do you need "create if missing, update if present"?

options.text: Incrementing a daily page-view counter
options.why: With (page_id, day) unique, `ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE SET views = views + 1` counts without a race.

options.text: Recording a user's last-active time (one row per user)
options.why: With user_id unique, an upsert creates or updates in one statement.

options.text: Creating an account if it doesn't exist, in order to deduct money from its balance
options.why: Deducting money is conditional (is the balance enough?); `UPDATE … WHERE balance >= n` is the right tool here.

options.text: Using ON CONFLICT on a column with no unique index
options.why: Detecting a conflict requires a unique index or constraint; without one, the statement fails.

questions.q: What is the problem in the code below?
questions.hint: What does the code do with the number execute() returns?

options.text: The order is confirmed even when the UPDATE changed no row (0)
options.why: Because it ignores the result, the order completes even with no stock. Throw an exception when `=== 0`.

options.text: With `stock >= 1` in the WHERE, stock will go negative in the database
options.why: That very condition prevents negative stock; the problem is in the code, not the database.

options.text: Writing stock = stock − 1 in DQL is not allowed
options.why: It is perfectly valid and a common atomic idiom.

questions.q: What is the best way to handle a seat during the 10 minutes of payment?
questions.hint: Think of both problems: losing the seat mid-payment, and a seat blocked by a user who walked away.

options.text: Book the seat only after payment succeeds
options.why: Someone else can take the seat during payment; the user is charged and then hears "sold out".

options.text: Block the seat forever as soon as it is chosen
options.why: The seats of people who leave without paying would never be released.

options.text: A 10-minute hold with an expiry; if it isn't confirmed in time, the seat is freed
options.why: The seat is guaranteed during payment, and abandoned holds expire on their own.

options.text: Hold the seat with a timer in the browser
options.why: Nothing is held on the server; a client-side timer doesn't hold a seat, it only shows the user the time.

questions.q: From which of these states can a reservation never return?
questions.hint: Think of the three paths out of held.

options.text: confirmed
options.why: A firm booking; this is a final state.

options.text: expired
options.why: The time ran out and the seat was released; the old hold never comes back to life, and you create a new one.

options.text: canceled
options.why: The user released it themselves; this is also a final state.

options.text: held
options.why: held is the only live state; from it you can go three ways.

questions.q: What does the index below guarantee?
questions.code:
CREATE UNIQUE INDEX one_active_reservation
    ON reservation (seat_id) WHERE status IN ('held', 'confirmed');
questions.hint: Which rows does the WHERE part apply the rule to?

options.text: A seat can have only one active (held or confirmed) reservation at a time
options.why: Expired or canceled rows fall outside the unique rule, so history can be kept.

options.text: Each seat will have only one reservation in its whole life
options.why: Because of the WHERE condition, only active rows are counted; the rest can pile up.

options.text: A user can hold only one seat
options.why: The index is only on seat_id, not on user_id.

options.text: A hold that has run out will expire on its own
options.why: An index changes nothing; stale rows must be expired first.

questions.q: A user trying to create a new hold keeps getting "seat taken", though the old hold on the seat expired long ago. What could be the cause?
questions.hint: When the time passes, does the record's status change by itself?

options.text: The row still says status = held, so the unique index treats it as active; it was not expired first
options.why: The passing of time doesn't change the status. Before creating a new hold, stale ones must be expired.

options.text: The database clock is wrong
options.why: The problem would exist even with a correct clock, because the status never changed.

options.text: The unique index shouldn't have a WHERE clause
options.why: A partial index is the right design; without it, the expired rows would be the blockers.

questions.q: Why is confirming safe in the code below, and what does `=== 0` mean?
questions.hint: The WHERE has two conditions.

options.text: 0 means the hold is no longer valid: it expired or was canceled
options.why: If the two conditions don't both match, no row changes. Then it cannot be confirmed.

options.text: 0 means the database was busy and a retry will do
options.why: The cause isn't busyness; the conditions didn't match. Retrying with the same expiry gives the same result.

options.text: 0 means the confirm succeeded, there was just nothing new to change
options.why: 0 means no row became confirmed. Treating it as success would make an expired hold look "successful" too.

questions.q: Which statements about the job that releases holds are true?
questions.hint: Who carries the responsibility for correctness?

options.text: Confirm and a new hold check expires_at themselves, so correctness holds even if the job is late
options.why: Expiry is checked at the moment of use; the job is only a broom.

options.text: With `#[AsPeriodicTask]` in Symfony Scheduler, you can run it regularly
options.why: If the class is invokable, the attribute alone schedules it; you only need to keep a scheduler worker running.

options.text: If the job misses a run, the seat stays blocked forever
options.why: A new hold first clears the stale ones, so the seat doesn't stay blocked.

options.text: Without the job, the expires_at column is useless
options.why: expires_at is the truth about expiry; it works in confirm and in holds even without the job.

questions.q: Ryan's payment succeeds 2 minutes after his hold expired, and Kevin has meanwhile held the seat. What should the system do?
questions.hint: How many rows will the confirm UPDATE change?

options.text: Confirm Ryan and cancel Kevin's hold, because Ryan paid
options.why: Kevin's hold is valid; forcing the payment through over everyone creates a new injustice.

options.text: Treat Ryan's confirm as failed, send a refund and ask him to pick a new seat
options.why: The CAS returns 0. Refunding the money and telling him clearly is the right course.

options.text: Give both the same seat and sort it out later
options.why: That is exactly double-booking, which this whole design exists to prevent.

options.text: Leave the payment as it is and tell nobody anything
options.why: The user's money has been taken and nobody has told them anything: the worst possible state.

questions.q: What is the biggest danger in this code?
questions.hint: What if something happens after flush() but before the dispatch?

options.text: If the process dies after the flush, the order exists but nobody learns of OrderPlaced
options.why: It writes to two separate systems; a failure in the gap leaves one committed and the other not.

options.text: If the dispatch is slow, the flush will fail
options.why: The flush was already committed, so a slow dispatch has no effect on it.

options.text: Doctrine will create the same order twice
options.why: That has nothing to do with this; the problem is a lost message, not a duplicate order.

questions.q: Which are valid reasons to avoid 2PC?
questions.hint: What happens when the coordinator fails, and do outside systems understand XA?

options.text: If the coordinator fails, participants are stuck holding locks
options.why: After saying yes to PREPARE, they can't decide for themselves.

options.text: Email, SMS and outside HTTP APIs usually don't support 2PC
options.why: Today's apps often talk to systems like these, which makes 2PC useless.

options.text: It is slow because of network round trips in every phase and locks held longer
options.why: Locks stay held longer, so performance drops and collisions rise.

options.text: Data never commits with 2PC
options.why: When it runs properly, it commits. The problems are getting stuck on failure and its narrow applicability.

questions.q: In an outbox design, why are the order and the outbox row written in the same transaction?
questions.hint: What would happen if one committed and the other didn't?

options.text: So both commit together or both are canceled, and the message is never lost
options.why: Only a database transaction gives atomicity, and here both rows are in the same database.

options.text: So the message is sent exactly once
options.why: An outbox gives at-least-once; with the relay's retries, the same message may go out twice.

options.text: So you no longer need a queue
options.why: You still need the queue: the relay reads the outbox and sends to it.

options.text: So 2PC can be used
options.why: An outbox is an alternative to 2PC, not an application of it.

questions.q: The relay sent a message to the broker but died before setting `published_at`. What happens next?
questions.hint: Will the row look "unpublished" again?

options.text: The message is lost and nobody ever receives it
options.why: The row is still unpublished, so it is sent again on the next pass; the message is not lost.

options.text: The message is sent again, so consumers must handle duplicates
options.why: This is at-least-once behavior, which is why consumers must be idempotent.

options.text: The database deletes the row itself
options.why: A database never does that on its own; only your code changes it.

questions.q: In a four-service saga (order, payment, stock, courier), the courier step fails. What is the right response?
questions.hint: The payment charge is already committed in another database.

options.text: Call ROLLBACK on all databases at once
options.why: The services have already committed their own transactions; a single rollback is impossible.

options.text: Release the stock hold, refund the payment, mark the order canceled, in reverse order
options.why: Each step runs its own compensation, from the back to the front.

options.text: Do nothing and ask the customer to order again
options.why: Leaving the charge and the stock hold in place does real harm.

options.text: Only mark the order canceled
options.why: The money and the stock hold haven't been returned: the customer loses money and stock stays blocked.

questions.q: A saga is undoing its steps and the refund call times out. What is the right behavior?
questions.hint: The customer's money is still taken. Can the saga just move on?

options.text: Retry the refund with growing waits, and alert a person if retries run out
options.why: The refund is still owed, so it must keep trying and must never fail silently.

options.text: Use the saga id as the refund's idempotency key, so a repeated attempt can't pay twice
options.why: A retry may run the refund again; the key makes the second run harmless.

options.text: Skip the refund and continue with the remaining undo steps
options.why: The order would be canceled but the customer's money stays taken.

options.text: Give up silently after the first timeout
options.why: A timeout is usually temporary. Giving up without retries or an alert leaves the customer out of pocket unnoticed.

questions.q: In the code below, what does `$fresh === 0` mean?
questions.hint: When does ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING insert no row?

options.text: This message id was already processed, so skipping the work is safe
options.why: A unique conflict means the work was done in an earlier pass.

options.text: The database connection failed
options.why: A failed connection would raise an exception, not return 0.

options.text: The message arrived in the wrong format
options.why: The format has nothing to do with it; this is a duplicate check.

questions.q: Which of these are parts of a correct idempotent consumer?
questions.hint: What does the handler do to deal with duplicates?

options.text: Inserting each message's id into a unique table
options.why: That unique constraint is the tool that catches duplicates.

options.text: Keeping the work and the "done" marker in the same transaction
options.why: They commit together, so you never get "marker saved but work not done".

options.text: Collecting seen ids in a PHP static array inside the handler
options.why: Every worker is a separate process, and nothing is remembered after a restart.

options.text: Treating the broker as exactly-once and keeping the handler simple
options.why: Ordinary brokers give at-least-once; duplicates will come.
